## Our Research Questions <i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i>

1.  Can **general-purpose LLMs** accurately evaluate sentiment in French texts **without fine-tuning**?
2.  How do **open-source** LLMs perform compared to closed-source?
3.  Does the **language of the prompt** (French vs. English) affect performance?

::: {.notes}
State the three core questions very clearly. These guide the rest of the presentation.
~30 seconds.

## The Experiment: 3 Conditions <i class="fas fa-flask"></i>

```{.mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph "Condition 1: Native"
      A1[French Prompt] --> B1(French Text);
      B1 --> C1[<i class='fa-solid fa-flag'></i> → <i class='fa-solid fa-flag'></i>];
    end

    subgraph "Condition 2: Cross-Lingual Prompt"
      A2[English Prompt] --> B2(French Text);
      B2 --> C2[<i class='fa-solid fa-flag-usa'></i> → <i class='fa-solid fa-flag'></i>];
    end

    subgraph "Condition 3: Translation-Based"
      A3[English Prompt] --> B3(English Translation);
      B3 --> C3[<i class='fa-solid fa-flag-usa'></i> → <i class='fa-solid fa-flag-usa'></i>];
    end
````

*Testing native understanding, cross-lingual ability, and impact of translation.*

::: {.notes}
Explain the purpose of each condition using the diagram. FR-FR tests native ability. EN-FR tests the cross-lingual prompt hypothesis. EN-EN checks performance on translated text.
\~45 seconds.
:::

## Guiding the LLMs: The Prompt Structure <i class="fas fa-scroll"></i>

```{.markdown .code-overflow-wrap .smaller}
Please analyze the sentiment of the following French text and provide a single
numerical rating according to this scale:

Sentiment Scale:
-1.0: Strong negative sentiment...
// ... (Scale definitions) ... //
 1.0: Strong positive sentiment...

Important instructions:
1. ...consider cultural and linguistic nuances...
2. ...analyze emotional tone, word choice...
3. Respond ONLY with a single numerical value...
4. Do not include ANY explanations...

Here is the text to analyze: [TEXT]
```

*(Consistent instructions, clear scale, strict output format)*

::: {.notes}
Show the structure, don't read the whole prompt. Emphasize key parts: clear task, defined scale, instruction for numerical output only, mention of cultural nuance. Highlight consistency across 19k prompts.
\~30 seconds.
:::

## Finding 2: Prompt Language? Minimal Impact <i class="fas fa-arrows-left-right"></i>

**Performance Across Linguistic Conditions (Average Correlation)**

| Condition          | Avg. Correlation | Avg. F1 (3-cat) | Avg. MAE (Lower is better) |
|--------------------|-----------------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| **🇫🇷 → 🇫🇷** (Fr/Fr) | 0.430           | 0.489           | 0.346                    |
| **🇬🇧 → 🇫🇷** (En/Fr) | **0.436** | **0.501** | **0.332** |
| **🇬🇧 → 🇬🇧** (En/En) | 0.418           | 0.494           | 0.357                    |

**Insight:** <i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i>

  - English prompts on French text (EN→FR) slightly edged out others.
  - **BUT:** Differences were marginal, not statistically significant.
  - **Takeaway:** For French, prompt language choice seems less critical. Direct analysis (FR→FR or EN→FR) slightly better than translation (EN→EN).

::: {.notes}
Address RQ3. Show the table comparing conditions.
Highlight that EN-\>FR was technically best but the difference wasn't significant.
Contrast this with literature suggesting strong English prompt advantage elsewhere.
Conclude that for this task/language, it matters less than expected. Direct analysis is slightly preferable to translation.
\~1 minute.
:::

## Finding 3: Broad Strokes <i class="fas fa-thumbs-up"></i>, Fine Details <i class="fas fa-magnifying-glass"></i><i class="fas fa-thumbs-down"></i>

**Classification Accuracy (F1 Score - Higher is better)**

![F1 Scores Comparison Across Models and Categories](about:sanitized){fig-align="center" height="450"}

**Key Points:** <i class="fas fa-chart-simple"></i>

  - **Huge jump** from 7-category (nuance) to 3-category (polarity) F1 scores.
  - Avg. F1: **0.302** (7-cat) ↗ **0.495** (3-cat) - **\~64% increase\!**
  - Models excel at **Positive / Neutral / Negative**.
  - Struggle with "somewhat positive/negative".

::: {.notes}
Show the F1 comparison chart (ideally side-by-side bars for 3 vs 7 cat per model/condition).
Emphasize the large performance difference.
State clearly that models are good at basic polarity but bad at fine-grained distinctions.
Mention the specific difficulty with intermediate categories.
\~1 minute.
:::

## So What? Practical Implications <i class="fas fa-wrench"></i>

**For Social Scientists:**

  - <i class="fas fa-check"></i> **Use LLMs:** Top closed & larger open models work *without fine-tuning*.
  - <i class="fas fa-comments"></i> **Prompt Flexibility:** French or English likely fine; direct analysis slightly better.
  - <i class="fas fa-bullseye"></i> **Focus on Polarity:** Rely on Pos/Neut/Neg (3-cat); cautious w/ nuance (7-cat).
  - <i class="fas fa-code-compare"></i> **Consider Trade-offs:**
      - **LLMs:** Nuance <i class="fas fa-arrow-right"></i> Transparency <i class="fas fa-arrow-down"></i>
      - **LSD:** Transparency <i class="fas fa-arrow-up"></i> Nuance <i class="fas fa-arrow-right"></i> Polarity <i class="fas fa-check"></i>

::: {.notes}
Summarize the key takeaways for the audience.
Provide actionable advice: Which models to use, how to prompt, what level of analysis to trust.
Reiterate the LLM vs. LSD trade-off clearly.
\~1.5 minutes.
:::

## Conclusion: Bridging the Language Gap <i class="fas fa-flag-checkered"></i>

**Can general-purpose LLMs analyze sentiment in French without fine-tuning?** **Yes.** <i class="fas fa-thumbs-up"></i>

**Key Takeaways:**

  - Leading LLMs offer powerful, *accessible* analysis.
  - Open-source models viable (bigger = better).
  - Prompt language less critical here.
  - Basic polarity = <i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i>; Fine nuance = <i class="fas fa-question-circle"></i>.
  - **LSD remains strong & transparent** for polarity & macro-trends.

**The Bottom Line:** Choose based on **nuance vs. transparency**. LLMs are valuable tools for non-English text.
